final.title: Human-in-the-loop means one clear approval rule
final.body:
If you are rethinking human-in-the-loop design, start with one recurring workflow and answer a plain question: which decision must stay with you before the output can take effect? That is the control boundary. For a small business, the useful split is not “AI or no AI”; it is filter, route, or approve. AI can sort, extract, or draft. Human approval stays where the consequence is real: money movement, customer commitments, legal or financial risk, or anything outside a simple template.

Bareni’s own demos show the shape of this, not customer results. In the accounts-payable demo, payment blocking and human-only approval are part of the design, and the blocked payment is a manual simulation on synthetic data. In the knowledge assistant demo, sources are shown so the answer is grounded instead of guessed. Both point to the same rule: let the system do the repetitive checking, but keep the last gate human when the decision matters.

A practical next step is to write one sentence for a single workflow: “AI may draft or flag this item, but I approve anything that moves money or changes a commitment.” If you cannot write that sentence clearly, the workflow is not ready yet. That is usually where the trouble starts, and the spreadsheet develops opinions.
